```{r setup}
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  comment = "#>",
  collapse = TRUE
)

options(crayon.enabled = FALSE, width = 78)

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(biplotEZ)
  library(plotly)
})

if (requireNamespace("devtools", quietly = TRUE)) {
  devtools::load_all(".", quiet = TRUE)
} else {
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(bipl5))
}

species_cols <- c("#1B9E77", "#D95F02", "#7570B3")
species_pch  <- c(16, 17, 15)

# Render a bipl5 plotly widget as a FIXED-SIZE canvas.
#
# reveal.js scales each slide with a CSS `transform: scale()`. plotly's
# responsive handler re-reads its container size on every window resize --
# and a transformed container reports an inflated size on large screens,
# so plotly redraws bigger and the (already transformed) widget overflows.
#
# Setting an explicit layout width/height with autosize = FALSE and
# disabling the responsive listener makes plotly draw once at a fixed
# pixel size; reveal.js then scales that canvas proportionally with the
# rest of the slide, at any window size.
stage <- function(bp, height = 560, width = 1100, ...) {
  p <- plot(bp, ...)
  p <- plotly::layout(p, width = width, height = height, autosize = FALSE)
  p <- plotly::config(p, responsive = FALSE)
  p$width  <- width
  p$height <- height
  p
}
```

## Today's Goal

[`bipl5` turns PCA, CVA, regression and PCO biplots into **interactive Plotly htmlwidgets**.]{.lead}

In this webinar we cover three things:

- Build a biplot directly with the **standalone `bipl5` workflow**.
- **Wrap an existing `biplotEZ` object** and render it with `bipl5`.
- Drop the resulting widget straight into a **Quarto presentation**.

. . .

All examples use the `iris` data set.

# Standalone Construction {.divider background-color="#1B9E77"}

[Part 1 — building a biplot from raw data]{.divider-tag}

## Build the Biplot {.smaller}

`init_biplot()` ingests the data and `scale_mds()` chooses the method and
subspace. Grouping aesthetics are set in the pipeline with `format_samples()`.

```{=html}
<style>
.reveal .code-build { justify-items: start; align-items: start; }
.reveal .code-build > * { grid-area: 1 / 1; width: 100%; margin: 0; }
.reveal .code-build pre { margin: 0; }
</style>
```

```{r standalone-build}
#| echo: false
library(bipl5)
library(biplotEZ)

bp_standalone <- init_biplot(iris) |>
  scale_mds(type = "pca", eigenvectors = c(1, 2)) |>
  format_samples(stratify = "col", by = Species, col = species_cols)
```

::: {.r-stack .code-build}

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
```r
bp_standalone <- init_biplot(iris)
```
:::

```

```

## The Standalone Plot

```r
plot(bp_standalone)
```

```{r standalone-plot}
#| echo: false
stage(bp_standalone, height = 560)
```

## Styling the Sample Layer {.smaller}

`format_samples()` restyles the rendered sample layer — no rebuild needed.

```{r standalone-format}
#| results: hide
bp_species <- bp_standalone |>
  format_samples(
    stratify = "col",
    by = Species,
    col = species_cols
  ) |>
  format_samples(
    stratify = "symbol",
    by = Species,
    pch = species_pch
  )
```

Colour and plotting character are set per group from the `Species` factor.

## Styled Biplot

```r
plot(bp_species)
```

```{r styled-plot}
#| echo: false
stage(bp_species, height = 560)
```

## A Second Stratifying Variable {.smaller}

`format_samples()` can stratify by **two different variables at once** — colour
by one, plotting symbol by another. The sample traces are rebuilt internally as
the observed `Species × Band` combinations, with a separate legend section per
variable.

```{r dual-stratify}
#| results: hide
iris_banded <- iris
iris_banded$Band <- factor(
  rep(c("A", "B", "C", "D"), length.out = nrow(iris_banded))
)

bp_dual <- init_biplot(iris_banded) |>
  scale_mds(type = "pca", eigenvectors = c(1, 2)) |>
  format_samples(stratify = "col", by = Species, col = species_cols) |>
  format_samples(stratify = "symbol", by = Band, pch = c(15, 16, 17, 18))
```

## Two-Variable Stratification

```r
plot(bp_dual)
```

```{r dual-stratify-plot}
#| echo: false
stage(bp_dual, height = 560)
```

## Adding More Displays {.smaller}

A single object can hold several displays. `append_mdsDisplay()` adds another
eigenvector pair to the dropdown.

```{r append-displays}
bp_multi <- bp_species |>
  append_mdsDisplay(c(1, 3)) |>
  append_mdsDisplay(c(2, 3))

names(bp_multi$meta$pc_info)
```

## Multi-Display Biplot

::: {.small-note}
Switch eigenvector pairs live with the dropdown in the top-left of the widget.
:::

```r
plot(bp_multi)
```

```{r multi-display-plot}
#| echo: false
stage(bp_multi, height = 530)
```

## Traversing the Object {.smaller}

`extract()` and `remove_mdsDisplay()` navigate a multi-display object.

```{r traversing-code}
bp_one_view   <- extract(bp_multi, mdsDisplay_13)
bp_without_23 <- remove_mdsDisplay(bp_multi, mdsDisplay_23)

iris_scores <- extract(bp_multi, mdsDisplay_12$Data$sample_coordinates)
head(iris_scores, 5)
```

## An Extracted View

::: {.small-note}
`bp_one_view` keeps only the PC 1 – PC 3 display pulled from the multi-display object.
:::

```r
plot(bp_one_view)
```

```{r extracted-view-plot}
#| echo: false
stage(bp_one_view, height = 530)
```

## Fit-Panel Layout {.smaller}

`overlay_fit()` stores a plotting preference: render the fit summaries as an
overlay across the full plot width rather than in a side panel.

```{r overlay-fit}
#| results: hide
bp_overlay <- bp_multi |>
  overlay_fit()
```

Open the **fit panel** from the widget toolbar to see the effect.

## Overlay Fit

```r
plot(bp_overlay)
```

```{r overlay-fit-plot}
#| echo: false
stage(bp_overlay, height = 560)
```

# biplotEZ Wrapper {.divider background-color="#D95F02"}

[Part 2 — when you already have a biplotEZ pipeline]{.divider-tag}

## Wrapping a biplotEZ Pipeline {.smaller}

Use `wrap_bipl5()` when your starting point is an existing `biplotEZ` pipeline.

```{r wrapper-pca-build}
#| results: hide
bp_ez_pca <- biplotEZ::biplot(iris[, 1:4]) |>
  biplotEZ::PCA() |>
  wrap_bipl5()
```

`wrap_bipl5()` consumes the `biplotEZ` object and returns a `bipl5` object —
ready for `plot()` and every traversing function.

## Wrapped PCA Biplot

```r
plot(bp_ez_pca)
```

```{r wrapper-pca-plot}
#| echo: false
stage(bp_ez_pca, height = 560)
```

## Wrapped CVA — Build {.smaller}

The same wrapper handles a CVA biplot; just pass the class variable.

```{r wrapper-cva-build}
#| results: hide
bp_ez_cva <- biplotEZ::biplot(iris[, 1:4]) |>
  biplotEZ::CVA(classes = iris$Species) |>
  wrap_bipl5()
```

## Wrapped CVA Biplot

```r
plot(bp_ez_cva)
```

```{r wrapper-cva-plot}
#| echo: false
stage(bp_ez_cva, height = 560)
```

## Regression Biplot — Build {.smaller}

A regression biplot calibrates axes onto an **externally supplied** sample map.
Here the target is a Sammon scaling of the `rock` data.

```{r wrapper-reg-build}
#| results: hide
target_map <- MASS::sammon(dist(scale(rock)), trace = FALSE)$points

bp_ez_reg <- biplotEZ::biplot(rock) |>
  biplotEZ::regress(Z = target_map) |>
  wrap_bipl5()
```

## Regression Biplot

```r
plot(bp_ez_reg)
```

```{r wrapper-reg-plot}
#| echo: false
stage(bp_ez_reg, height = 560)
```

## Spline Axes — Build {.smaller}

`PCO(axes = "splines")` calibrates **non-linear** axes — useful when a straight
axis would distort how a variable maps onto the display.

```{r wrapper-spline-build}
#| results: hide
bp_ez_spline <- biplotEZ::biplot(rock, scale = TRUE) |>
  biplotEZ::PCO(axes = "splines") |>
  wrap_bipl5()
```

## Spline-Axis Biplot

```r
plot(bp_ez_spline)
```

```{r wrapper-spline-plot}
#| echo: false
stage(bp_ez_spline, height = 560)
```

## Alpha-Bag Biplot — Build {.smaller}

`biplotEZ` enhancements survive the wrap. Adding `alpha.bags()` to the pipeline
draws an **alpha bag** around each group, and `wrap_bipl5()` carries it through.

```{r wrapper-bags-build}
#| results: hide
bp_ez_bags <- biplotEZ::biplot(iris[, 1:4], group.aes = iris$Species) |>
  biplotEZ::PCA() |>
  biplotEZ::alpha.bags() |>
  wrap_bipl5()
```

## Alpha-Bag Biplot

```r
plot(bp_ez_bags)
```

```{r wrapper-bags-plot}
#| echo: false
stage(bp_ez_bags, height = 560)
```

# Wrap-Up {.divider background-color="#7570B3"}

[What to demonstrate live]

## What to Show Live {.smaller}

- **Hover** over observations to see the original `iris` measurements.
- Use the **dropdown** to switch between stored eigenvector displays.
- **Click** an observation to draw prediction lines onto the calibrated axes.
- Use the **legend** to toggle sample groups, axes, translated axes and densities.
- Open the **fit panel** on PCA biplots for supporting summaries.

## Takeaway

::: {.takeaway}
`plot()` returns a **Plotly htmlwidget**, so the same `bipl5` object works
interactively in RStudio, saves as standalone HTML, embeds in Quarto
documents, and presents in a Quarto slide deck — from one code path.
:::

. . .
